title: The Burning of the Rice Fields
text:
In a story told by Lafcadio Hearn, an old man named Hamaguchi Gohei was the most respected man in a Japanese fishing village. His house stood on a high terrace above the bay, and from it he looked down on the village and the beach below. It was harvest time, and his rice stood stacked in the fields around his house, ready to bring in. Down by the shore the villagers were preparing for a festival.

One evening there was a long, slow earthquake. Hamaguchi, watching the sea, saw it suddenly run back from the shore, uncovering the sand far out. The villagers ran down onto the beach to stare at it. He understood that a great wave was coming and that there was no time to warn them.

He took a burning torch and set fire to his own rice stacks, one after another. The temple bell was rung, and seeing the fire on the hill, the villagers came running up to help, as was their duty. Hamaguchi stood over the burning harvest and would not let them put it out. Then he pointed to the sea. The wave struck, and the village below was swept away. But the people were on the hill.

Hamaguchi had made himself poor to save them. The grateful villagers rebuilt their homes and his, and while he still lived they built a shrine to him and worshipped his spirit as a living god.
lesson: Sometimes the only way to get people to move fast is to sacrifice something of your own that they can see. Act on the danger you can see before others recognize it.
source: Lafcadio Hearn, A Living God, in Gleanings in Buddha-Fields (1897)
caveat: Hearn based the story on Hamaguchi Goryo and the 1854 tsunami in Hiro, Wakayama, where the real man burned rice straw to guide villagers to safety in the dark, as the tsunami was striking.
